{
  "persuasion": "PERSUADED",
  "support_scope": "CORE_ONLY",
  "rationale": "The book's core identification of the great fish as a devouring kingdom that swallows and is forced to give back is the best-supported reading of the specific printed references (Jer 51:34; Ezek 32:2) and the Jonah/Matthew evidence once the book's method of cross-text symbol consistency is applied. The strongest counter (tomb/Sheol as death-realm type of Christ's burial) explains the three-day duration and Jesus' explicit comparison, but it does not account for the empire-dragon language of swallowing-and-vomiting that the cited texts share with Jonah's itinerary, nor for the kingdom-scale of the appointed ketos. Secondary scene-by-scene Passion details and the Jerusalem-as-heart-of-the-earth claim are elaborations that go beyond the core and remain open to dispute.",
  "book_core_identification": "The great fish (dag gadol / ketos) is a devouring kingdom that swallows and is forced to give back.",
  "book_secondary_elaborations": [
    "Jerusalem (spiritually Egypt/Sodom) is the specific kingdom/dragon that swallowed the Messiah, riding Rome as the beast.",
    "Heart of the earth = Jerusalem (navel/midst of the nations), so the three days measure time under arrest in the city rather than time in a tomb.",
    "Full scene-by-scene Passion prophecy table (fare, sleep, lots, reeds, sailor worship, etc.).",
    "Jonah's prayer naming 'yeshuah' and the Red-Sea reeds as further micro-symbolism.",
    "Nineveh's repentance and Jonah's anger as the gospel going to the nations and Israel's envy."
  ],
  "strongest_counter_interpretation": "The great fish is the realm of death/Sheol/the grave (or God's appointed instrument of judgment and preservation that places Jonah in a death-like state), typologically prefiguring Christ's burial and resurrection for three days and nights as Jesus himself states in Matthew 12:39-40.",
  "counter_core_identification": "Great fish = death/Sheol/tomb (or the instrument that effects a death-like descent and deliverance), the sign of Jonah being the three-day burial and rising of the Son of Man.",
  "counter_relation_to_book_core": "CONTRADICTS",
  "material_core_denial": "The counter denies that the primary referent of the fish is a kingdom/empire that swallows peoples and is forced to disgorge them; it treats the fish instead as the place or state of death (or a non-political providential agent) whose only indispensable symbolic content is the three-day confinement that Jesus cites.",
  "counter_case": [
    "Jesus himself supplies the controlling parallel: three days and nights in the whale's belly = three days and nights in the heart of the earth (Matt 12:40), language that points to burial/death rather than political conquest.",
    "Jonah's own prayer equates the fish with 'the belly of Sheol' and 'the bottoms of the mountains' with bars, classic underworld imagery (Jonah 2:2, 6).",
    "The fish is 'prepared/appointed' by the LORD (Jonah 1:17) as an instrument of both judgment and deliverance, not identified inside Jonah as any empire.",
    "Mainstream Christian reception has long treated the episode as resurrection typology (supported also by the Lukan emphasis that Jonah himself was a sign of repentance), without needing the empire-swallowing reading.",
    "The Jer 51:34 and Ezek 32:2 dragon/whale metaphors for Babylon and Pharaoh are real but apply the sea-monster image to hostile kings; they do not automatically redefine Jonah's dag gadol as a kingdom rather than a death-realm."
  ],
  "book_explanatory_advantages": [
    "Directly accounts for the two printed references (Jer 51:34; Ezek 32:2) that describe kingdoms as dragons/whales that devour, fill the belly, and cast out—language that maps onto Jonah's swallow-and-vomit itinerary.",
    "Preserves symbol consistency: fish scale with sea (peoples/nations) to yield a great body of men = kingdom, matching the book's method of deriving terms from multiple OT witnesses.",
    "Explains why the fish is 'appointed' yet still functions as a hostile power that God overrules and forces to release its prey (cf. Jer 51:44 'I will bring forth out of his mouth that which he hath swallowed up').",
    "Integrates the sign of Jonah as more than duration: the whole sequence of swallowing by a kingdom-power, confinement, and forced release anticipates the Passion and resurrection without reducing the fish to a mere container."
  ],
  "counter_explanatory_advantages": [
    "Rests on the most explicit New Testament statement (Matt 12:40) linking the fish to the heart of the earth / burial.",
    "Fits Jonah's internal description of the belly as Sheol and the language of corruption and being brought up (Jonah 2; cf. Ps 16 / Acts 2).",
    "Requires fewer cross-text leaps; the typology is self-contained within Jonah + the Gospel citations and has been the dominant Christian reading for centuries.",
    "Avoids the need to identify a specific historical kingdom inside the fish itself."
  ],
  "evidence_book_core_cannot_explain": [],
  "comparative_winner": "BOOK",
  "decisive_sources": [
    "Jeremiah 51:34 (Babylon swallows like a dragon, fills belly, casts out)",
    "Ezekiel 32:2 (Pharaoh as whale/dragon in the seas)",
    "Jonah 1:17; 2:1-10 (appointed great fish, belly of Sheol, vomited out)",
    "Matthew 12:39-41 (sign of Jonah: three days in the fish = three days in the heart of the earth)",
    "Jeremiah 51:44 (God forces the swallow-er to give back what it swallowed)"
  ],
  "unresolved_objections": [
    "Whether the fish must be identified with Jerusalem (or Jerusalem-plus-Rome) rather than a more generic devouring power or the death-realm that any kingdom ultimately serves.",
    "Whether 'heart of the earth' is better read as Jerusalem's navel rather than the conventional grave/Sheol sense that Jesus' wording most naturally suggests.",
    "The full scene-by-scene Passion table and the three-days-in-the-city calendar solution go beyond the core and are not required to accept the devouring-kingdom reading of the fish.",
    "The method assumes high uniformity of symbols across distant texts; a more atomistic reading can treat the Jer/Ezek dragons as mere political metaphors without redefining Jonah's fish."
  ],
  "confidence": "medium"
}
